references.text: Zechariah prophesied about the thirty pieces of silver as the price set on the Lord – a remarkable parallel to the chief priests agreeing to give Judas money (ἀργύριον) to betray Jesus. See [ref:Zech 11:12|Zechariah 11:12].

Matthew's parallel account gives more details about the agreement between Judas and the chief priests, including that the sum was thirty pieces of silver. Judas asked what they would give him, and they weighed out thirty silver coins. See [ref:Matt 26:14-16|Matthew 26:14-16].

After Jesus' judgment, Judas regretted his actions and brought the thirty pieces of silver back to the chief priests and elders – the same money (ἀργύριον) that was agreed upon in Luke 22:5. See [ref:Matt 27:3-5|Matthew 27:3-5].

Mark's parallel account tells that the chief priests were glad (ἐχάρησαν) when Judas came to them, and they promised to give him money – exactly the same event as in Luke 22:5. See [ref:Mark 14:10-11|Mark 14:10-11].

John tells that the devil had already put it into the heart of Judas Iscariot to betray Jesus, which provides the background for why Judas went to the chief priests and made an agreement about money. See [ref:John 13:2|John 13:2].

Peter mentions in his speech that Judas bought a field with the reward he received for his wickedness – a direct consequence of the money agreement made in [ref:Luke 22:5|Luke 22:5]. See [ref:Acts 1:18|Acts 1:18].

Paul's warning that love of money is the root of all evil is concretely illustrated in Judas' case: his desire for silver (ἀργύριον) led to history's greatest betrayal. See [ref:1 Tim 6:10|1 Timothy 6:10].
